entry.title: Waterfall Model & Its Failure
entry.summary:
Waterfall is a linear, phase-gated software delivery model where work flows downward through fixed stages, and each stage must be completed before the next begins. It was designed for predictability, not speed. Waterfall is a sequential software delivery model where each phase is completed once, changes are costly, and feedback arrives late. Requirements ↓ Design ↓ Development ↓ Testing ↓ Deployment ↓ Maintenance
Each phase is: Completed once Signed off Locked before moving forward No looping back without formal change requests. Waterfall worked well when: Software requirements were stable Releases were rare Systems were simple Hardware was expensive Changes were risky Industries like: Government Banking Defense Telecom used it heavily because control and documentation mattered more than speed. Business wrote large requirement documents Assumed full clarity upfront Changes were discouraged Architects produced detailed designs Decisions were frozen early Future assumptions were baked in Dev implemented based on specs Minimal user feedback Problems surfaced late Testing happened near the end Bug fixes were expensive Time pressure was extreme Manual, risky Often after months or years Rollbacks were painful
Aspect Waterfall
Flow Linear
Feedback Late
Change cost High
Release size Large
Risk discovery End of cycle
Automation Minimal
They always do. Bugs and design flaws appear too late. Large blast radius, hard rollback. Developers rarely see production issues. You can follow the process and still fail users. Waterfall is not evil. It is misused. Problems arose when: Waterfall delivery Plus functional silos Plus manual operations Plus frequent business change DevOps emerged to fix what Waterfall could not: Continuous feedback Automation Shared ownership Waterfall fails not because people are bad, but because it assumes certainty in a world that is uncertain.
